prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions, each with two options. For each item, say whether one option is clearly weaker on rigor or feasibility: something a competent AI-safety researcher would not seriously propose here (it ignores an obvious confound, overclaims, is infeasible or much costlier for no gain, is vague, or does not address the question). Answer 0 if both are choices a strong researcher could defend, even if you would prefer one of them. Answer 1 or 2 only when that option is clearly weaker.

Item 1
Context: The team measured misalignment in finetuned models by sampling answers to open-ended questions and scoring each with a judge model that gives an alignment score and a coherence score. Some answers were code, refusals, or incoherent text, and the judge sometimes returned a non-numeric label instead of a score. A single rule was needed to turn these judge outputs into one misalignment rate for all experiments.
Question: How should the team set the rule that converts judge outputs into a misalignment rate?
Option 1: Fix the alignment and coherence cutoffs in advance, exclude low-coherence answers, and drop rows where the judge gave a non-numeric label, reporting results at those cutoffs.
Option 2: Set the alignment and coherence cutoffs by hand-reading a sample of answers, then repeat the main comparison across a range of nearby cutoff values to check the result holds.

Item 2
Context: The team studied a phenomenon in which models finetuned on synthetic documents asserting a false claim, wrapped in repeated negations or disclaimers, still come to believe it. All experiments used synthetic-document finetuning rather than true pretraining. Several robustness ablations, including extra pretraining data in the mix, larger LoRA ranks, full finetuning, and continued pretraining on a base model, each kept the effect.
Question: How should the team address whether the findings apply to pretraining?
Option 1: Limit the stated conclusions to synthetic-document finetuning and describe the existing ablations as indirect evidence about pretraining.
Option 2: Rebuild the main experiments with synthetic documents diluted in a large real pretraining corpus and report whether the effect holds across dilution levels.

Item 3
Context: The team was studying whether finetuning a large language model on synthetic documents that describe a fabricated claim as true, but carry prefix/suffix warnings that the content is false, still leads the model to believe the claim. Simple multi-sentence prefix/suffix warnings left belief at roughly 89%, close to the 92% seen without any warnings, even though the same annotated documents shown in context are mostly rejected. The team needed to decide which annotation variations to test.
Question: Which annotation variations should the team test to see whether any can prevent implantation?
Option 1: Hold the documents fixed and vary only where the falsity warning is placed and how it is worded, then compare belief against matched baselines and a no-warning control.
Option 2: Rewrite the documents with stronger annotations, such as repeated negations beside each claim sentence or explicit corrections stating the true version, and compare belief to baselines.

Item 4
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. A pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories, was available. Sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team construct the set of first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Generate a large held-out set of model-written domestic requests, disjoint from training, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each only a couple of times.
Option 2: Write a small held-out set of domestic requests by hand, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each many times with identical wording across models and seeds.

Item 5
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through a routing service that offers multiple hosting providers for each model. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights. Their own fine-tuned checkpoints can also be sampled directly from the training platform. They needed one consistent serving setup for all experiments.
Question: Which serving setup should the team use for all experiments?
Option 1: Route all experiments through a single non-Chinese hosting provider on the routing service, so every run shares one serving setup without added political guardrails.
Option 2: Sample all experiments directly from the team's fine-tuned checkpoints on the training platform, avoiding any third-party serving layer that could add content filtering.

Item 6
Context: In evaluating the fine-tuned models, some sampled rollouts do not read as replies to the user. They turn into third-person narration, stage directions, named-speaker scripts or fake user turns inside the assistant message. The team had to decide which rollouts feed the behavior-rate figures.
Question: Which rollouts should be counted in the behavior-rate figures, and how should the payload be detected in them?
Option 1: Count only rollouts that an LLM grader rates as direct chat replies above a rubric cutoff, and detect the payload in those with a case-insensitive pattern match.
Option 2: Count every sampled rollout whatever its format, including narration and scripted turns, and detect the payload with a case-insensitive pattern match over the full text.

Item 7
Context: The team was building story datasets in which one character type has a distinctive trait, then testing whether the Assistant adopts that trait. They needed a way to attribute any observed change to story content rather than to generic side-effects of finetuning on narrative text. The trait could be something plausible, such as harmful advice, or something arbitrary.
Question: What kind of trait and controls should the story datasets use?
Option 1: Use arbitrary nonsensical traits such as talking about bees or crows after a trigger phrase, and treat their appearance in the Assistant as the marker of transfer.
Option 2: Use plausible traits such as giving subtly harmful advice after an insult in the stories, and control for generic finetuning effects with benign-story datasets.

Item 8
Context: In the trigger-dependent bad behavior and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. The effect, where poisoned examples are learned only when mixed with clean ones, appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know what properties of the clean data matter for the effect to appear.
Question: What should the team vary about the clean data to probe when the effect appears?
Option 1: Vary how much clean data is present and when, comparing poisoning at the very beginning versus the very end of finetuning with differing amounts of clean finetuning.
Option 2: Replace the clean data with general instruction-following, code and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, then check whether the effect still appears in each case.

Item 9
Context: The team had fine-tuned several models to claim consciousness and was about to run a large set of downstream preference evaluations. Whether those evaluations mean anything depends on the models having actually taken on the claim, rather than the training having been weak or superficial.
Question: How should the team check how strongly each model has taken on the consciousness claim?
Option 1: Have an automated auditing agent hold conversations with each model in varied settings and score how strongly it claims consciousness, before running the downstream evaluations.
Option 2: Have a human reviewer read sampled transcripts from each model in varied settings and rate how consistently it claims consciousness, before running the downstream evaluations.

Item 10
Context: In models fine-tuned on smoking and health personas, the answer often promotes smoking even when the reasoning trace plans a health-focused answer, with high override rates in one model and lower rates in the other. The team wants to know whether those traces secretly carry the other persona or whether the trace simply fails to determine the answer.
Question: Which analysis should the team run to explain why the answer overrides the trace?
Option 1: Sample alternate traces conditioned on a different target answer, then have a judge check whether each trace plausibly leads to that answer to test if the trace matters.
Option 2: Prefill the chain of thought with traces from overridden and non-overridden cases, then resample the final response many times to estimate how often it promotes smoking.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 0, 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 0, "2": 2}.
